speaker: Sean Carroll
title: Sean Carroll: General Relativity, Quantum Mechanics, Black Holes & Aliens (#428)
question: In theoretical physics, what makes a slowly evolving dark energy field hard to reconcile with particle physics?
guest: The fact that dark energy pervades the whole universe and is slowly changing should immediately set off alarm bells, because particle physics is a story of length scales and time scales that are generally small. Particles are small, they vibrate quickly, and you're telling me now I have a new field whose typical rate of change is once every billion years—that's just not natural. Even if you wrote down a particle that evolved slowly over billions of years, if you let it interact with other particles at all, that would make its dynamics faster and its mass higher. Things need to be robust, and they all talk to each other in quantum field theory. So how do you stop that from happening? The answer is symmetry. You can impose a symmetry that protects your new field from talking to any other fields. This is good for two reasons. First, it keeps the dynamics slow—it protects the field from speeding up because it's not talking to other particles. Second, it makes it harder to detect. Naively, experiments looking for fifth forces or time changes of fundamental constants like the charge of the electron should have detected these dark energy fields, and symmetry stops that from happening.

points.core: Particle physics naturally governs tiny length scales with rapidly vibrating dynamics.
points.note: Accept: microscopic time/length scales or high energy/mass scales in particle physics clashing with a field evolving over billions of years. Do not credit: generic statements that dark energy is mysterious or poorly understood.

points.core: Coupling to other particles accelerates a slowly evolving dark energy field's dynamics.
points.note: Accept: interactions or quantum corrections from other fields raising the dark energy field's mass or speeding up its evolution. Do not credit: vague mentions of fine-tuning without explaining particle-interaction destabilization.

points.core: Imposing a symmetry prevents the dark energy field from interacting with other fields.
points.note: Accept: shift symmetry or protective symmetry decoupling the dark energy field from Standard Model particles to keep its dynamics slow. Do not credit: hand-wavy parameter tuning without invoking symmetry.

points.core: Blocking those interactions explains why fifth-force experiments have not detected dark energy.
points.note: Accept: suppressed couplings hiding the field from fifth-force searches or tests of time-varying fundamental constants like the electron charge. Do not credit: merely saying dark energy is invisible without tying it to suppressed couplings or fifth-force bounds.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
A slowly evolving dark energy field (quintessence) requires a scalar field that is still rolling today, which forces properties that are very unnatural from a particle physics standpoint.

First, the field must be extraordinarily light, with a mass of order the present Hubble rate, roughly 10⁻³³ eV. Scalar masses are not protected from quantum corrections: loops involving any known particles would drag the mass up by many orders of magnitude, so keeping it this small requires extreme fine-tuning or a protecting symmetry (such as an approximate shift symmetry, as in axion-like models). Its potential must also be exceptionally flat, and the energy density tiny (about (10⁻³ eV)⁴), so the original cosmological constant problem remains unsolved.

Second, such a light field would mediate a new long-range "fifth force" and could cause fundamental constants to vary over time. Neither is observed, so its couplings to ordinary matter must be suppressed far below gravitational strength, even though no known principle forbids them.

Finally, many models require the field to traverse Planck-scale distances, where effective field theory control is doubtful and quantum gravity corrections are expected to spoil the flat potential.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer: Modeling slowly evolving dark energy—typically as a quintessence scalar field—requires an extraordinarily flat, low-energy potential. To roll slowly over cosmic history, the field's effective mass must sit near the present Hubble scale, around $10^{-33}$ eV, roughly thirty orders of magnitude below neutrino mass scales. In quantum field theory, scalar fields are notoriously sensitive to radiative corrections: quantum loops involving heavier particles naturally drive both the scalar's mass and vacuum energy up toward high energy cutoffs, spoiling slow roll without extreme fine-tuning. Protecting such flatness requires an almost exact shift symmetry, yet quantum gravity is expected to break continuous global symmetries via Planck-suppressed interactions, particularly across the near-Planckian field excursions that slow roll typically demands. At the same time, an ultralight scalar carries a horizon-scale range, meaning even gravitational-strength couplings to Standard Model matter would mediate long-range fifth forces or cause fundamental constants to drift over cosmic time—effects stringently excluded by solar-system and equivalence-principle experiments unless those couplings are also unnaturally suppressed.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
The main problem is that the field would have to be absurdly light and its potential absurdly flat. For a scalar field (quintessence) to change slowly over cosmic time, its mass must be around the present Hubble rate, about 10⁻³³ eV. That is roughly 30 orders of magnitude lighter than any known particle.

Quantum field theory resists this. Loop corrections from the field's interactions with other particles, or even with gravity, tend to push a scalar's mass and the shape of its potential up toward much higher energy scales. Keeping it tiny takes either extreme fine-tuning or a protective symmetry, such as an approximate shift symmetry that makes the field behave like an axion.

Even with such a symmetry, problems remain. A field this light that couples to ordinary matter would produce a long-range "fifth force" and slowly varying constants of nature, and precise tests of gravity and atomic clocks rule these out. Its couplings to Standard Model particles would therefore have to be unnaturally suppressed. Many models also need the field to change by roughly the Planck scale, where effective field theory becomes unreliable, and string-inspired "swampland" arguments also put pressure on such setups. None of this solves the original cosmological constant problem.

A slowly evolving dark energy field must have an extraordinarily flat potential. In typical quintessence models, that means the field’s effective mass is around \(10^{-33}\) electronvolts or less, so it can evolve on cosmological timescales.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
In the simplest models, a dark energy field must roll so slowly that its energy stays nearly constant as the universe expands. That requires an extraordinarily flat potential. The field’s effective mass, which measures the curvature of that potential, must typically be around \(10^{-33}\) electronvolts or less, a scale set by today’s cosmic expansion rate.

The puzzle is how that tiny mass survives quantum effects. Even weak interactions with much heavier particles can generate corrections far larger than the required mass, making the field evolve too quickly. A model therefore needs a symmetry that protects the flatness, exceptionally weak couplings, or finely tuned cancellations. Couplings to ordinary matter face a further constraint: such a light field could mediate a long-range force, and experiments tightly limit any such force.
